newsitem.title: USA: Criminal probe of FBI files witnesses denied.
newsitem.headline: Criminal probe of FBI files witnesses denied.

text.p: A Treasury Department official denied Monday that two Secret Service agents who testified to Congress in the FBI files affair were the subjects of a potentially criminal investigation.

The two agents testified in defence of the accuracy of Secret Service lists of White House personnel -- blamed by the White House for a "bureaucratic snafu" that resulted in the improper acquisition of FBI files on hundreds of Republicans.
Republicans suggested at a Senate hearing that the two agents, John Libonati and Jeff Undercoffer, were being victimised for giving testimony damaging to the White House.
But Valerie Lau, Inspector General of the Treasury Department which oversees the Secret Service, told an Appropriations subcommittee the two were not under investigation.

"These two agents are not the subject of an investigation. We are focussing on the preparation of testimony ... that led to a conclusion that the Secret Service could not provide a list of outdated names (to the White House)," Lau said.
Reports that the two agents were under potentially criminal investigation followed an Oct. 21 meeting between members of the inspector general's staff and Secret Service officials.
But Lau, asked if the words "criminal investigation" had been used at the meeting, said she believed it was the Secret Service that had used these words, but "we sought to clarify the situation."
Emily Coleman, regional inspector general for investigations, who was at the meeting, said the Secret Service had insisted on asking if a criminal probe was under way.

She said she responded that the investigation was in the preliminary stages and that she did not know if it would turn out to be an administrative, civil or criminal case. Any criminal case would be handled by independent counsel Kenneth Starr, who is investigating the FBI files affair.

Lau said the investigation was a fact-finding mission launched in response to inquiries by Representative Cardiss Collins, an Illinois Democrat and member of a House committee that heard the two agents' testimony, and Sen. Ted Stevens, an Alaska Republican who is a senior member of the Appropriations Committee.
Sen Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican, said after the hearing he had not been satisfied with the answers.
"It smacks of political retribution and possibly intimidation of witnesses," he said of the investigation.
"The timing, scope and generation of this investigation give credence to the notion that this I.G. inquiry is simply politically motivated payback," Sen. Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican, said.
